newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Palm-talk of EMU delay "totally misplaced".
newsitem.headline: Buba's Palm-talk of EMU delay "totally misplaced".

text.p: Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm said on Monday recent speculation about a possible postponement of the introduction of the single currency, scheduled for January 1, 1999, was "totally misplaced."

Palm also said it was better for European Union states to refrain from creative accounting and thereby slightly exceed the budget deficit criterion rather than to keep within the limit by resorting to budget tricks.

He was convinced a majority of European Union (EU) states had a good chance of meeting the convergence criteria on monetary union, Palm said according to a statement from the central bank of Baden-Wuerttemberg of which he is president.
The bank released the statement ahead of a speech Palm was due to hold on monetary union.

Palm said an early postponement would do lasting damage to European integration, impair efforts to curb government spending and hurt the German economy through the "massive" appreciation of the mark that would probably follow a delay.

"Whether it makes sense to start monetary union on January 1, 1999 and which countries should take part is to be decided in the spring of next year on the basis of realised data from 1997 -- and not today on the basis of speculative assumptions," Palm said according to the statement.
"The issue and the timetable of European monetary union must not be pushed to an fro like in a shunting yard."

Speculation about a delay has grown after one of Germany's leading economists, Herbert Hax, said at the weekend Bonn would in all likelihood miss the Maastricht treaty's budget deficit and public debt goals this year.

Under the treaty, states seeking to qualify for monetary union must keep their budget deficits below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997. But the treaty allows for leeway in certain circumstances.

"From Palm's point of view a trick-free deficit of just over three percent in 1997 that will be further reduced in following years due to savings efforts is preferable to 2.9 percent reached through creative accounting," the statement said.

The German government aims to reduce its budget deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP this year but many economists doubt it will be able get its finances in shape sufficiently given steady growth in unemployment.
Palm noted that Germany in particular had to get its house in order since it was the only EU member not to have reduced its deficit in 1996.
He fully agreed with the European Monetary Institute's insistence that states must achieve sustained convergence on the basis of lasting savings efforts, the statement said.
Palm also said financial markets expected a fairly large number of EU members would able to launch the single currency on time.
The convergence of bond yields across Europe towards the low German levels showed markets saw no danger of inflation for years to come.

"One expects the euro -- a euro within a larger currency union -- but a euro that will be hard. A flight out of the mark or out of the euro in future would therefore be ill-considered and would not be in line with the market's assessment."
